source_title: What Dry and Off-Dry Means in Wine Plus the Other Sugar Descriptors
newsletter_intro:
Wine labels can feel a little intimidating at first, but they’re actually trying to help you. Once you understand a few sugar terms, it gets a whole lot easier to pick the bottle you actually wanted.

And yes — fruity does not automatically mean sweet. Let’s clear that up.

slide 4: Residual sugar is what’s left after fermentation

instagram_reel.script:
Quick wine myth to clear up: fruity does not automatically mean sweet.

A wine can smell like cherries, peaches, or tropical fruit and still be totally dry. Those flavours usually come from the grape itself — not leftover sugar.

What matters is residual sugar. That’s the sugar left after fermentation, when yeast has done its job.

So if you’ve ever picked up a Riesling expecting crisp and dry, then realized it was off-dry, that’s the label working exactly as it should.

Once you know what dry and off-dry mean, shopping gets way easier. And way less confusing.

linkedin.post:
Wine labels can feel overly technical at first, but they do serve a real purpose: helping people buy the style they actually want.

One of the most useful things to understand is residual sugar. That’s the sugar left in wine after fermentation, and it’s what helps explain terms like dry and off-dry.

A common misconception is that fruity means sweet. It doesn’t. A wine can show cherry, peach, or tropical fruit character and still be completely dry. Fruit flavour and residual sugar are two different things.

That distinction matters for consumers, but also for retailers, educators, and hospitality teams trying to guide people toward a better fit.

The more clearly we talk about wine style, the less intimidating the category becomes — and the easier it is for people to make choices with confidence.
